Am I required to buy it?

Federal law requires it only in a high-risk zone (A or V) with a federally regulated or backed mortgage, or federal help to buy or build (42 U.S.C. §4012a). Outside those zones, a lender may still require it.

59.3% of Wisconsin's NFIP policy units are in high-risk zones (not 59.3% of all buildings, and not an answer about your own home).

Of the NFIP claim dollars paid here (1978–2026), 28.7% went to claims rated outside high-risk zones A and V. That uses the zone on each claim, not today's map, and leaves out claims with no zone.

Flood zonePolicy unitsShare
Zone AE (high-risk)5,47849.1%
Zone X4,51040.5%
Zone A (high-risk)9808.8%
Other high-risk zones (AH, A03, VE, AO and others)1511.4%
Other low-risk or unclassified zones300.3%

Policy records keep the code they were rated with, so older labels such as A1 to A30 are counted on their own. Every zone starting with A or V is high-risk; A1 to A30 and AE are the same kind of area (44 CFR §64.3).

Insured units by the zone each policy is rated in. How this is counted What each means: zone AE, zone X, zone VE. Find yours with the flood zone map lookup by address.

Not in the NFIP (58 communities here): Adell; Alma Center; Arpin; Barneveld; Bruce; Cameron; Cedar Grove; Chenequa; Clear Lake; Clinton; Conrath; Couderay; Cuba City; Dickeyville; Downing; Eagle; Eagle River; Elderon; Fairchild; Fenwood; Francis Creek; Glen Flora; Glenbeulah; Granton; Hancock; Haugen; Hewitt; Ingram; Knapp; Lohrville; Lublin; Lyndon Station; Mason; Mattoon; Melvina; Mount Hope; Mount Horeb; Nelson; Neosho; North Bay; Oconomowoc Lake; Ogdensburg; Park Ridge; Redgranite; Ridgeland; Sheldon; Sherwood; Sister Bay; Tennyson; Tony; Unity; Vesper; Waldo; Warrens; Webster; Weyerhaeuser; White Lake; Williams Bay. Federal flood insurance (NFIP) is sold only in communities that take part in the NFIP; in a community that has not joined, or once a suspension takes effect, no one can buy an NFIP policy.

Flood insurance cost in Wisconsin

In Wisconsin, typically about $919 a year ($77 a month), fees included. Half of homeowners here pay between $617 and $1,355. To check a quote, use the checker at the top.

A quarter pay under $617 · Typical $919 · A quarter pay over $1,355 · A tenth pay $1,936 or more

Each policy's annual cost (premium plus the federal policy fee, reserve fund assessment and HFIAA surcharge), single-family primary residences. The bar is the middle half of policies, from 6,582 single-family primary-home policies. These are existing policies, many still below FEMA's full-risk price.

The NFIP also offers policies for renters and businesses. The median here is for single-family primary-home policies, not businesses or second homes. Renting? See what renters pay.

Source: floodsmart.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

How do I actually get covered — and how fast?

Most policies start 30 days after you buy. Bought while making, increasing, extending or renewing a mortgage, it can start at closing if the insurer is paid within 10 days (30 if the lender, title company or settlement attorney pays).

  • Waiting period30 days
  • Bought with a new or refinanced mortgageCan start at closing, if paid in time
  • NFIP building limit$250,000
  • NFIP contents limit$100,000

Most homeowners insurance does not cover flood damage. Does homeowners insurance cover flooding? To buy: call the NFIP at (877) 336-2627, go to FloodSmart.gov, or ask any licensed insurance agent. Every NFIP insurer offers the same rates.

Already flooded? Insured: report the loss to your insurance agent or company now (FEMA's steps: how to start a flood claim), and send a proof of loss (your signed, sworn statement of the amount you are claiming) within 60 days of the flood (44 CFR 61, App. A(1), Art. VII). Not insured: a policy bought today will not cover a flood that already happened, and FEMA disaster aid is open to people in counties designated in a federally declared disaster.

Wait exceptions, exclusions, premium increases and surcharges, aid, appeals, rebuilding and closing rules: the NFIP rules in full.

Your state's insurance regulator: Wisconsin Office of the Commissioner of Insurance.

Source: floodsmart.gov, agents.floodsmart.gov, fema.gov, ecfr.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

Flood insurance claims in Wisconsin: what floods pay out

Floods in Wisconsin have led to 9,192 NFIP flood claims and $140.9 million in payouts since 1978; the worst years were 2008, 2018 and 2025.

Bar height is dollars paid that year. Orange bars are the three costliest years: 2008 ($33,558,486), 2018 ($19,217,595), 2025 ($17,182,021). Total paid $140,894,641. Totals for 2025 and 2026 are not final while their claims stay open. How this is counted

Do flood claims here actually pay out?

Most do: 78.2% of claims in Wisconsin paid something. The average paid claim was $19,908 (all years, in dollars of the day, not adjusted for inflation).

Typical claim: the median paid building claim was $6,525.

  • Average paid claim, incl. code-upgrade (ICC) pay$19,908
  • No recorded payment21.8%
  • Claims that paid7,186
Decade of the floodClaims filedShare that paid something
1970s47074.9%
1980s88259.0%
1990s2,39177.5%
2000s2,55281.7%
2010s1,98481.4%
2020s91383.6%

FEMA's claim records give a reason when a building claim has no recorded payment, such as damage less than the deductible, not an actual flood, seepage or backed-up drains. The average is over claims that paid something and includes Increased Cost of Compliance payments (help to elevate or rebuild to code), which the yearly totals above leave out. Dollars are as paid at the time, not adjusted for inflation; a single home can file across several floods over the years. All years, records FEMA coded as entered in error left out (the claims page uses losses from 2020 on, so its shares differ). FEMA's data has no open or closed field, so a recent claim with no payment may still be paid.

Would a policy here pay to rebuild my home?

Not in full for at least 32.7% of the 3,644 single-family policies here that report a rebuilding cost: FEMA's records put it above the NFIP's $250,000 building limit.

  • Rebuilding cost above the building limit (of 3,644 policies reporting one)32.7%
  • Single-family policies insured to the building maximum (all of them, not only those above)50.4%
  • Damage was more than the coverage (of 6,962 claims paid with a damage figure)4.4%

The two shares have different bases: insured-to-the-maximum counts every single-family policy with the full building limit; the rebuilding-cost share counts only the policies that report a rebuilding cost. Homes insured for less than their own rebuilding cost can also fall short. How this is counted

The NFIP pays the cost to rebuild (not a depreciated value) only for a single-family home that is your principal residence and is insured for at least 80% of its full rebuilding cost, or for the $250,000 maximum.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies; FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Claims. Data effective August 31, 2026; retrieved November 14, 2026.

What does it cost in my flood zone?

From about $480 a year (Zone AH) to $1,073 (Zone AE) here. Your zone is on your lender's flood determination or FEMA's map; find its row below.

Flood zoneMedian / yrPriced policies
Zone AE$1,0733,296
Zone X$7552,749
Zone A$932419
Zone AH$48063

What the zone codes mean (44 CFR §64.3): A, AE and A1–A30 are high-risk; AO and AH are high-risk with shallow flooding; A99 is high-risk behind a flood barrier FEMA treats as complete; V, VE and V1–V30 are coastal high-risk, flooded by tides with fast-moving water (velocity); B and X are areas of moderate flood hazard, C and X areas of minimal hazard; D has possible but undetermined flood hazards. A 1 percent or greater chance a year works out to a 26% or greater chance of at least one such flood over 30 years.

Why can a high-risk zone cost less than Zone X here? The premium is based on the flood risk of the building. The reason for any one zone is not in this data.

Zones with fewer than 50 priced single-family policies are omitted. Your own premium still depends on elevation and coverage.

Source: ecfr.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

Why do sites quote different prices for Wisconsin?

Because they measure different things. Existing single-family policies here typically cost $919 a year, and policies first bought in the past year $776; other sites count other policies, years or averages.

MeasureAmountWhat it counts
Typical cost, single-family homes (median)$919premium plus fees; the middle policy
Typical premium only$718before the federal fee, reserve fund and surcharge
Typical cost, policies whose term began Jan–Aug 2026$9494,337 policies
Typical cost, policies first bought in the past year$7761,042 policies, past year
FEMA's full-risk premium (median)$763the price FEMA's model sets for these existing policies
Full-risk premium plus average fees$993what these existing policies would cost at FEMA's full price
Average (mean) cost, single-family homes$1,109pulled up by a few expensive policies
Average cost, every policy type$1,324adds condos, rentals and businesses

Condo owners: condo-unit policies are 2.7% of NFIP policy units here and whole condo buildings 1.6%. The every-policy-type average includes them. Condo-unit policies here have a median cost of $433 a year (premium plus fees, 305 priced policies; condo flood insurance by state). The single-family figures leave out every policy FEMA marks as a condo unit or a whole condo building.

All from the NFIP policies in force on August 31, 2026. How this is counted

How do current premiums compare with FEMA's full-risk price?

30.6% of single-family primary-home policies in Wisconsin have a premium below FEMA's full-risk premium by any amount, so those policies' bills are rising toward it. Median premium $718, full-risk $763 (premiums only, before fees).

  • Median premium charged (before fees)$718
  • Median full-risk premium$763
  • Pay below full-risk30.6% of 6,582

Yearly cap: By law, most premium rates may not rise more than 18% a year (42 U.S.C. §4015(e)).

Source: agents.floodsmart.gov, govinfo.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

How Wisconsin appears in the national research papers

Each paper measures one thing in FEMA's records for every U.S. county with enough records. A fifth is a position in a list, not a grade or a prediction.

  • Flood damage over building coverage: NFIP claims by county: 1 of this state's counties have at least 100 paid single-family primary-home claims with recorded damage and coverage and are listed.
  • Outside the zone: paid flood claims rated outside high-risk zones: 2 of this state's counties have at least 100 claims with a payment and a rated zone and are listed.
  • Building deductibles on record: NFIP single-family homes by county: 42 of this state's counties have at least 30 single-family primary-home policy units with a known building deductible and are listed.
  • Peak month of NFIP claims by county: 5 of this state's counties have at least 100 NFIP claims with a month of loss and are listed.
  • The gap to FEMA's full-risk premium: NFIP single-family homes by county: 42 of this state's counties have at least 30 single-family primary-home policies priced both ways and are listed.

Do the same homes flood again here?

Yes: FEMA's disaster-aid records hold 65,241 records from homes here that FEMA lists as flood-damaged in more than one declared disaster; 9,411 records are from homes FEMA's disaster-aid data flags as severe repeat-loss (SRL).

  • Disaster-aid records on repeat-flood homes65,241
  • Records from homes flagged severe repeat-loss (SRL)9,411

These count records, one per home per declared disaster, not distinct homes, and FEMA does not mark flood damage on every record. How this is counted

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Individual Assistance Multiple-Loss Flood Properties. Data: FEMA's current multiple-loss list; retrieved November 14, 2026.

How often is Wisconsin a flood disaster?

39 federal disasters for floods or storms here; the latest was Severe Storms, Tornadoes, and Flooding (2026).

  • June 2026 — Severe Storms, Tornadoes, and Flooding
  • September 2025 — Severe Storms, Straight-Line Winds, Flooding, and Mudslides
  • March 2020 — Severe Winter Storm and Flooding
  • August 2019 — Severe Storms, Tornadoes, Straight-Line Winds, and Flooding
  • October 2018 — Severe Storms, Tornadoes, Straight-Line Winds, Flooding, and Landslides
  • August 2018 — Severe Storms, Straight-Line Winds, and Flooding

Only the latest are listed, newest first; disasters with the same month and title share one line, which says how many; the count covers every flood, hurricane, tropical-storm and coastal-storm declaration FEMA lists here, plus severe-storm declarations whose title names flooding, including emergency declarations. How this is counted

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Disaster Declarations Summaries. Data: declarations through 2026; retrieved November 14, 2026.

Did FEMA aid homeowners after floods and storms?

Yes: FEMA approved $310.3 million for homeowners here after floods and storms, about $3,611 per registration.

FEMA disaster aid helps with uninsured and underinsured losses, and is separate from NFIP insurance. The average is over every registration, including those approved for nothing. Only disasters counted in the flood-disaster card are included; their aid can still cover wind or tornado damage from the same storm. Disasters for COVID, fire, winter storms or tornadoes alone are left out.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Housing Assistance (Owners). Data: homeowner aid by disaster; retrieved November 14, 2026.

Are these counts complete?

Every record FEMA's download lists was received and counted.
